diagram_classification: Theological / biblical-exegetical (a schematic plan of a sacred space, probably the Temple or city of Jerusalem with its gates, read allegorically)
interpretation: The diagram is a set of concentric circles, in red and black ink, with rectangular gate-cartouches set into the outer rings at the cardinal and intermediate points. The innermost circle holds the words 'Habitatio Legis et Sacerdotium' (dwelling of the Law and of the priesthood). This marks the centre as the sacred core: the Temple or Tabernacle, with the Law and the priestly office. The surrounding ring carries red labels. Some are legible, such as 'Habitatio' and 'Prophetia', and others are only partly legible, perhaps including 'Moabitis' and 'Amon'. These seem to name the groups or functions arranged around the centre. The outer rings are pierced by gates, one of which reads 'Porta Aquilonis' (north gate), and others seem to carry names such as Ioseph, Iuda or Ruben, and perhaps 'Iosaphat'. This suggests gates named after the tribes or places of Israel, as in the vision of the city in Ezekiel 48 or in descriptions of Jerusalem. The diagram probably presents an orientated, ordered sacred topography. The Law and priesthood sit at the centre, prophecy and other peoples or functions surround them, and the tribal or directional gates give access from the four quarters. A typological or allegorical reading of Jerusalem and the Temple as the Church is likely, but the fragmentary text prevents a firm identification of the exact source text.
evidence: Visible: concentric circles, a central inscription 'Habitatio Legis et Sacerdotium', labels in the middle ring ('Habitatio', 'Prophetia' and others partly legible), and gate-cartouches in the outer rings, one reading 'Porta Aquilonis', placed at the cardinal and intermediate points. External: this layout resembles medieval plans of the Temple, Tabernacle or the city of Ezekiel's vision with tribal gates, and such plans were often read allegorically. Several inscriptions are abraded, rotated or abbreviated and could not be read with confidence, so the identification of the specific gates, peoples and source text remains uncertain.
